catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.6.2 'Timing', pp. 38-46; three principles and 'not phonemic' pp. 38-39; bisyllable/trisyllable rules pp. 39-40; four-syllable pp. 41-42; five- and six-syllable pp. 42-43; seven-to-eleven-syllable examples pp. 44-45; author's summary p. 45; global stress pp. 45-46; restatement p. 103 (p. 128): 'Primary stress is preferentially placed on a penultimate syllable and upon a long vowel.'
catalog_quote: Worrorra is an anticipatory stress-timed language ... An account of stress patterning in Worrorra needs to observe three important principles: (i) stress is attracted to long vowels, (ii) primary stress is attracted to the penultimate syllable, and (iii) global stress patterns usually override local stress and readjust it. However there is quite a bit of variability around these principles, such that primary stress may be moved to a long vowel not in penultimate position, or to a penultimate vowel that is not long. ... stress is not phonemic in Worrorra, and few words display invariant stress. ... In bisyllabic words the penultimate stress rule applies almost absolutely, regardless of length variations, producing a trochaic foot ... Trisyllabic words fall into three categories. Most of these words show stress on their first syllable, in a dactylic foot ... Trisyllabic words with a long vowel in the final syllable may show stress on that syllable, in an anapaestic foot ... A number of other words, however, show stress on the penultimate syllable in an amphibrach foot. These include words with a long vowel in penultimate position ... The predominant stress pattern overall seems to require stress on the first, and then on alternate syllables, in a trochaic or dactylic metre ... the penultimate stress rule appears to be fairly unusual in Australia, and this coupled with the influence of syllable length results in an irregular and interesting suprasegmental phonology.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No contrastive stress. Primary stress prefers the penultimate syllable and is attracted to long vowels; when these conflict either may win, so placement varies. Bisyllables are trochaic almost without exception; trisyllables are mostly initial-stressed (dactyl), but take penult stress when the penult vowel is long and may take final stress when the final vowel is long; longer words parse into trochaic/dactylic feet with primary stress normally in the final (penult-headed) foot. Phrase-level ('global') rhythm and rhetorical emphasis readily override word-level placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses (grave accent) fall on the heads of the other feet, typically the first syllable and alternate syllables thereafter (trochaic/dactylic metre); a long antepenultimate vowel often takes secondary stress before a primary-stressed penult; the primary/secondary distinction 'is not rigidly maintained'.
new_statements.exceptions: Bisyllabic exceptions iyáaw 'castigate' and kulnmérr 'tail' (truncated from kulnmérrba); a small set of words with lexically specified amphibrach stress (e.g. jinálya 'spear', wulúrrku 'charcoal', realis forms of =bwa 'fall' which keep stress on the root); the progressive suffix -(y)eerri attracts primary stress; polymorphemic words 'inherently variable' (kàrranangkánya ~ kàrranángkanya); optional final vowels shift the pattern (dambéema ~ dámbeem).
new_statements.domain_note: Patterns described for words in citation/recitation style (slow-to-moderate speech); certain suffixes and postposed elements ((-)aalb, (-)ngurru, -nangka, -rnanya, -(y)eerri, -(kw)aal) are inside the phonological word and affect foot boundaries; in connected/rapid speech 'global' (phrasal, rhetorical) stress supplants word-level stress. Author notes the penultimate rule is unusual for Australia.
new_statements.identity_note: Clendon 2014 describes Worrorra proper (worr1237) as spoken by the last fluent speakers (Patsy Lalbanda, Amy Peters, Daisy Utemorrah) recorded at Mowanjum/Derby; spelling 'Worora' in the 2000 thesis and in Love's works is the same language. Capell & Coate 1984 treat Worora within a Northern Kimberley comparative frame (file held by the project is held under ngar1284 because it was downloaded for Ngarinyin).
